Tesla Inc. will add an extra production shift to finish outstanding Cybertruck orders before it dismantles the line next year.

On Saturday, CEO Elon Musk said in a post on X that the backlog is "far more than Tesla can make" before the line comes down around June or July next year. "We will add an extra shift to try to get all orders done in time."

Cybercab Takes Priority in Tesla's AI Pivot

Musk said a day earlier that Tesla would wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas factory and shift resources toward the Cybercab, a two-seat robotaxi, according to Reuters.

The Cybercab plays a key role in Musk's plan to transform Tesla from an automaker into a company focused on AI and robotics.

Musk's latest comments follow criticism from investor Ross Gerber, CEO of Gerber Kawasaki Wealth & Investment Management, who called the wind-down "another failure" in a post on X. Fellow investor Gary Black wrote on X that Tesla missed an opportunity by not building a more conventional-looking pickup.

Trending: Avoid the #1 Investing Mistake: How Your 'Safe' Holdings Could Be Costing You Big Time

Cybertruck Sales Run Far Below Musk's Target

The Cybertruck began reaching customers in late 2023 but has struggled to meet Musk's early expectations.

Tesla's "other models" category, which includes the Cybertruck, totaled 8,295 deliveries in the third quarter, according to a Benzinga analysis of the company's data. That is the most Cybertrucks Tesla could have sold in the period.

The figure implies annualized sales of 28,000 to 32,000 units. At the high end, that is about 13% of Musk's 250,000 annual goal.

The stainless steel pickup has also faced repeated recalls and quality concerns since launch. Its unconventional design limited prospects in overseas markets, including Europe.

title: Tesla Bull Predicts Democrats Will “Block Autonomy,” a Bigger Risk Than Data Centers
detail:
Tesla Bull Predicts Democrats Will “Block Autonomy,” a Bigger Risk Than Data Centers
David Hanson
Tue, November 10, 2026 at 10:06 AM MST 5 min read
TSLA
GOOGM
Trade Tesla on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Tesla Bull Predicts Democrats Will "Block Autonomy," a Bigger Risk Than Data Centers ©Spencer Wood's Images, Roberto Nickson from Pexels via Canva
Key Takeaways

Jason Calacanis, a Tesla shareholder, said on This Week in Startups that after the midterms Democrats will "block autonomy," a bigger risk for tech than data centers.

The risk is bigger for Tesla than for Alphabet's Waymo, since Elon Musk says Cybercab will dominate only where the law allows it, and Tesla is moving Cybertruck out of Giga Texas to build more of them.

Tesla trades at 177x forward earnings against a five-year average of 108x, and analysts' 2028 EPS estimate of $3.24 is still below what it earned in 2022.

A presidential veto makes a ban unlikely. But a Democratic Congress can stall federal rules that would override the states, which leaves robotaxis winning approval one city at a time.

Since Democrats swept Congress last week, much of the talk in tech has been about data centers.

Angel investor Jason Calacanis sees a bigger target. "The biggest outcome of this midterm election is not data centers," he said on Monday's episode of This Week in Startups. "I think they're going to block autonomy."

That's a striking call from someone who disclosed buying 3,000 shares of Tesla (TSLA:NASDAQ) late last month. And Alphabet (GOOG) is exposed too, through Waymo, the service Calacanis pointed to as already cutting into human drivers' work.

Drivers vote, too

Calacanis's case starts with jobs. In the big Waymo markets, he said, the number of rides human drivers get "is going down a bit," though he called the data early and noisy. And Democrats' instinct, in his words, is "protect, protect, protect."

Anduril founder Palmer Luckey spelled out the stakes on X: take ride-hailing's "$150B+" of revenue "and subtract the cost of paying 16,000,000 drivers. That is the bet." Musk replied on Tuesday that "Cybercab will do a majority of all passenger miles in any jurisdiction where it is not prohibited by law."

Read that last part again. Musk's bull case comes with a legal condition, and the drivers Luckey wants to subtract are the people Calacanis expects Democrats to protect.

Investors are paying for Cybercab today

Musk posted on Oct. 17 that "Optimus and Cybercab will be the vast majority of Tesla's value." Later in the episode, Calacanis was asked how a law blocking autonomy would hit robot makers like Figure. His answer: "If that legislation comes out, the valuation of those companies gets cut in half." By Musk's own account, Tesla is one of those companies.

Tesla Inc. CEO Elon Musk said the automaker will refund Cybertruck deposits to many customers as it prepares to wind down production of the electric pickup, rejecting reports that the decision stems from unprofitability.

Musk Rejects Reports Of Cybertruck Unprofitability

"The Cybertruck order rate far exceeds our production rate," Musk clarified in an X post early Monday. "We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people."

The Cybertruck order rate far exceeds our production rate. We will try to make as many as possible before shutting down the line in about 8 months, but will have to return deposits for a lot of people.

"This is not a case of Cybertruck being unprofitable, as has been misreported by legacy media," Musk said, arguing that manufacturing complexity created an opportunity cost "vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production."

His remarks followed Tesla's November 6 announcement that Cybertruck production would end around mid-2027, freeing manufacturing capacity at Gigafactory Texas for its autonomous robotaxi. Reuters reported the decision that day.

Tesla Plans Additional Shift Before Shutdown

Musk's comments followed his Saturday announcement that Tesla would add another production shift to fulfill outstanding Cybertruck orders before dismantling the assembly line for Cybercab expansion.

However, the pickup's commercial performance has fallen short of earlier expectations. According to Kelley Blue Book figures, U.S. Cybertruck sales declined 48% to 20,237 vehicles in 2025, compared with Musk's earlier annual target of 250,000.
